court: The European Court of Human Rights (First Section)

facts.text: The case originated in an application (no. 38187/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights by Ms İlkay Adalı on 12 September 1997.

anchor.surface_text: 1.  The case originated in an application (no. 38187/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national living in the “Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus” (“TRNC”), Ms İlkay Adalı (“the applicant”), on 12 September 1997.

facts.text: The applicant alleged that her husband had been killed by Turkish and/or “TRNC” authorities and that the national authorities failed to carry out an adequate investigation into his death.

anchor.surface_text: 3.  The applicant alleged, in particular, that her husband had been killed by the Turkish and/or “TRNC” authorities and that the national authorities had failed to carry out an adequate investigation into his death.

facts.text: The applicant contended that following her husband's death she had been subjected to continuing harassment, intimidation and discrimination by the “TRNC” authorities.

anchor.surface_text: She further contended that, following the death of her husband, she had been subjected to continuing practices of harassment, intimidation and discrimination by the “TRNC” authorities.

facts.text: The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998 when Protocol No. 11 came into force.

anchor.surface_text: 4.  The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11).

facts.text: The applicant was born in 1944 and lives in Lefkoşa, northern Cyprus, in the “Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus” (“TRNC”).

anchor.surface_text: 12.  The applicant was born in 1944 and lives in Lefkoşa, in the northern Cyprus, “Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus” (“TRNC”).

facts.text: The application concerns the killing of the applicant's husband, Mr Kutlu Adalı, by unknown persons.

anchor.surface_text: 13.   The application concerns the killing of the applicant's husband, Mr Kutlu Adalı, by unknown persons.

facts.text: The applicant alleged serious involvement of Turkish and/or “TRNC” agents in the murder and complained about the inadequacy of the investigation by the “TRNC” authorities.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant made serious allegations about the involvement of Turkish and/or “TRNC” agents in the murder. She further complained of the inadequacy of the investigation launched by the “TRNC” authorities into the death of Kutlu Adalı.

facts.text: The applicant contended that her husband had received death threats on several occasions because of his articles and political opinions.

anchor.surface_text: She contended that her husband had received death threats on several occasions because of his articles and political opinions.

facts.text: The Government denied all allegations concerning the murder and maintained that the “TRNC” authorities had immediately commenced a thorough investigation but the perpetrators had not been identified.

anchor.surface_text: The Government denied all allegations concerning the murder of Kutlu Adalı. They maintained that the “TRNC” authorities had immediately commenced an investigation into his death, and had conducted a thorough investigation. However, the perpetrators of the crime had not yet been identified.

facts.text: The Government rejected the applicant's allegations of harassment and submitted these were mere speculation.

anchor.surface_text: The Government also rejected the applicant's allegations of harassment and submitted that these submissions were of mere speculation.

facts.text: Mr Kutlu Adalı was a Turkish Cypriot writer and journalist known for strongly criticising Turkish Government and “TRNC” authorities and advocating a united Cyprus.

anchor.surface_text: 18.  The applicant's husband, Mr Kutlu Adalı, was a Turkish Cypriot writer and journalist who was known for having written and published articles strongly criticising the policies and practices of the Turkish Government and the authorities of the “TRNC”. He had always claimed that Cyprus should not be divided and that Turkish and Greek Cypriots should live in a united republic based on a pluralist democratic system.

facts.text: Between 1961 and 1972, Kutlu Adalı was private secretary to Mr Rauf Denktaş, later President of the “TRNC”.

anchor.surface_text: 19.  Apart from his writing and journalism, Mr Kutlu Adalı had also held various civil service posts in the past. Between 1961 and 1972 he was employed as the private secretary to Mr Rauf Denktaş, who later became the President of the “TRNC”.

facts.text: In 1972, Kutlu Adalı's salary was suspended because he wished to write an article critical of Mr Denktaş's policies.

anchor.surface_text: In 1972 Mr Adalı's salary was suspended because he had wished to write an article about policies of Mr Denktaş with which he disagreed.

facts.text: Kutlu Adalı refused to work for Bayrak radio station controlled by Turkish Resistance Movement and was imprisoned without charge for one week.

anchor.surface_text: At that time, Mr Denktaş wanted the applicant's husband, Kutlu Adalı, to work for a radio station called Bayrak (Flag), which was under the control of the Turkish Resistance Movement. Mr Kutlu Adalı refused to work for this radio station and was imprisoned without any charge or trial for one week because of his refusal.

facts.text: In 1974, Kutlu Adalı was appointed Head of Identity Cards Section; suspended in 1979; reinstated in 1986 as adviser in Tourist Office; retired in 1987.

anchor.surface_text: In 1974 Mr Adalı was appointed to the post of Head of the Identity Cards Section of the Department for the Registration of the Population. In December 1979 he was suspended, and was reinstated in 1986, when he was given the post of adviser in the Tourist Office of the “TRNC”. His career as a civil servant ended in 1987, when he was compelled to take early retirement at the age of 50.

facts.text: Kutlu Adalı wrote under a pseudonym initially for safety, then under his real name from 1981, writing regularly for Yenidüzen newspaper for seven years before his death.

anchor.surface_text: During his public service and after his retirement Mr Kutlu Adalı continued his career as a writer and journalist. Initially, he wrote under a pseudonym (Kerem Atlı), because it was dangerous for him to express his political views about a unified Cyprus using his real name. In 1981 he started using his real name. For the last seven years before his death he wrote regularly for Yenidüzen, a left-wing newspaper.

facts.text: Between January 1980 and July 1996, Kutlu Adalı was subjected to harassment including attacks on his house and threatening phone calls.

anchor.surface_text: Between January 1980 and July 1996 unknown persons subjected the applicant's husband to various forms of harassment. His house was attacked with machine guns and he received frequent threatening phone calls.

facts.text: On 17 March 1996, Kutlu Adalı published an article about thieves breaking into St Barnabas monastery and linked the thieves to members of the Civil Defence Organisation.

anchor.surface_text: On 17 March 1996 the Yenidüzen newspaper printed an article by Kutlu Adalı about an incident in which thieves had broken into a tomb in the monastery of St Barnabas and stolen various objects of cultural significance. He had written that the licence plates and the colour of the thieves' cars had been noted, and the licence plates had been traced as belonging to two members of the Civil Defence Organisation.

facts.text: After the article, the editor of Yenidüzen received a threatening call from the head of the Civil Defence Organisation; Kutlu Adalı also received frequent threats.

anchor.surface_text: After the publication of this article, the editor of the newspaper received a threatening phone call from the head of the Civil Defence Organisation. Mr Adalı also began to receive frequent threatening phone calls.

facts.text: On 6 July 1996 at around 11.35 p.m., Kutlu Adalı was shot and killed in front of his house in the “TRNC” by unknown persons.

anchor.surface_text: On 6 July 1996, at around 11.35 p.m., the applicant's husband was shot and killed in front of his house in the “TRNC” by unknown persons.

facts.text: The applicant was in Istanbul on the night of the killing and had spoken to her husband at about 11.15 p.m., when he told her he was being threatened.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant was in Istanbul on the night when he was killed. When she had telephoned her husband at about 11.15 p.m., he had told her that “they” had been threatening him.

facts.text: The “TRNC” authorities refused to show the applicant her husband's body; she was told no post mortem had been carried out though the body had been rayed.

anchor.surface_text: The “TRNC” authorities refused to show the applicant her husband's body. She was told by the doctor in charge of the mortuary, Dr İsmail Bundak, that no post mortem had been carried out, although the body had been rayed.

facts.text: The applicant learned for the first time that a post mortem had been carried out from the Government's observations of 1 April 1999 and was provided a copy of the report.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant was informed for the first time that a post mortem had been carried out in the Government's observations of 1 April 1999, and a copy of the post-mortem report was provided.

facts.text: The applicant's neighbours told her that shortly before the killing a black car was parked in the street, similar to one driven by Altay Sayıl, a retired police officer.

anchor.surface_text: She found out from her neighbours that shortly before her husband's death, a black car had been parked in the street. This black car was of the same model as the car driven by Altay Sayıl, a retired police officer who had become friendly with the family in the last months of the applicant's husband's life.

facts.text: Neighbours heard Kutlu Adalı begging for his life and a man saying he deserved to die; street lighting went out at about 10.30 p.m. and was off until after the shooting.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant's neighbours told her that around the time her husband had been shot they had heard him begging his killers for his life. They said that they had heard a man saying that the applicant's husband deserved to die. The neighbours also informed her that the electric lighting in the street outside the applicant's home had gone out at about 10.30 p.m., causing the area to be in darkness, and had not been switched on again until shortly after Mr Adalı had been shot.

facts.text: Within minutes of the shooting, about twelve military cars arrived and sealed off the area; “special teams” of police threatened neighbours with guns to stay indoors.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant also learned from her neighbours that within only a few minutes of the shooting about twelve military cars had arrived and had sealed off the area, and that the “special teams” of police officers had threatened the neighbours with guns to force them to go back inside their houses.

facts.text: On 8 July 1996, the pro-“TRNC” newspaper Kıbrıs reported a statement from the Turkish Revenge Brigade claiming responsibility for the killing.

anchor.surface_text: On 8 July 1996 the pro-“TRNC” government newspaper Kıbrıs reported that it had received a statement from a fascist group calling itself the Turkish Revenge Brigade, claiming that it had killed Kutlu Adalı.

facts.text: Three days after the killing, the applicant's family received an anonymous call naming two individuals allegedly responsible for the murder; police refused to investigate.

anchor.surface_text: Three days after her husband was killed, the applicant's family received a telephone call from an anonymous caller, a woman, who gave the names of two individuals who she said were responsible for Mr Adalı's murder, a Mr Hüseyin Demirci and a man whose first name was Orhan. The applicant informed the police about this phone call but the police refused to start an investigation, stating that this woman was known for making false allegations to the police.

facts.text: On 14 July 1996, the applicant's children met the President of the “TRNC” requesting effective action to find the killer; the President promised to act.

anchor.surface_text: On 14 July 1996 the applicant's children arranged a meeting with the President of the “TRNC”. They requested him to take steps to ensure that effective action was taken to find their father's killer, and the President promised to take effective action.

facts.text: On 18 July 1996, the applicant requested President Denktaş to award martyr status to Kutlu Adalı; the request was rejected on 9 September 1996.

anchor.surface_text: On 18 July 1996 the applicant requested President Denktaş that the status of martyr be awarded to Kutlu Adalı. On 9 September 1996 her request was rejected.

facts.text: There were press allegations that Abdullah Çatlı, an extreme right-wing activist linked to the “Grey Wolves”, was involved in the killing; he allegedly arrived in “TRNC” under a false identity in early July 1996.

anchor.surface_text: There have also been repeated allegations in the press that a man called Abdullah Çatlı, an extreme right-wing activist who was linked with the “Grey Wolves” and who was allegedly instructed by some Turkish officials to kill people suspected of being PKK members, was involved in the death of the applicant's husband. According to the applicant's personal information, Abdullah Çatlı had arrived in the “TRNC” at the beginning of July 1996 under a false identity.

facts.text: In December 1996, the applicant complained to the security forces' commander that the investigation into her husband's death was inadequate.

anchor.surface_text: In December 1996 the applicant went to see the security forces' commander, Mr Hasan Peker Günal, and complained that the security forces were not investigating her husband's death properly.

facts.text: On 5 March 1997, Yenidüzen published a letter signed by the head of the “Grey Wolves” threatening left-wing journalists; the applicant gave copies to police but received no response.

anchor.surface_text: On 5 March 1997 the Yenidüzen newspaper published a letter signed by the head of the “Grey Wolves”, which contained a threat that left-wing journalists and writers would be killed like the applicant's husband. The applicant gave copies of this article to the police to investigate, but she did not receive any response.

facts.text: Plain-clothes policemen constantly followed the applicant and her daughter; their phones were tapped and correspondence monitored; they received anonymous calls and had phone/fax lines disconnected.

anchor.surface_text: Plain-clothes policemen have constantly been following the applicant and her daughter; their phones had been tapped and their correspondence monitored. They have received anonymous phone calls and their telephone and fax line has been disconnected from time to time.

facts.text: The “TRNC” regime refused to register the “Kutlu Adalı Foundation” aimed at furthering Kutlu Adalı's ideas on peace, democracy, human rights and freedom.

anchor.surface_text: The “TRNC” regime also refused to register an association, which is called “Kutlu Adalı Foundation”, whose aims include the furthering of the ideas of Kutlu Adalı regarding peace, democracy, human rights and freedom.

facts.text: The applicant's request to keep her husband's press card entitling her to privileges was rejected.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant also requested permission from the authorities to keep her husband's press card that entitled her to certain privileges, such as discounts for air fares. However, this request was also rejected.

facts.text: On 20 June 1997, public authorities prevented the applicant and her daughter from attending a meeting in southern Cyprus by denying permission to cross the border.

anchor.surface_text: On 20 June 1997 the public authorities prevented the applicant and her daughter from attending a meeting organised by a radio station in southern Cyprus, by not giving them permission to cross over to that side.

facts.text: On the anniversary of Kutlu Adalı's death, the applicant organised a ceremony; the municipality dug up the road under their street and a picture of Kutlu Adalı was stolen from their garden.

anchor.surface_text: On the anniversary of Kutlu Adalı's death the applicant organised a ceremony to commemorate her husband. On the day of the ceremony, the municipality brought in digging machines to dig up the road just under their street. The applicant also submits that a picture of Kutlu Adalı, which was displayed in their garden, was stolen.

facts.text: On 10 August 1997, the applicant heard three gunshots outside her home; a real-estate agent later urged her daughter to sell their house, believed to be sent by “TRNC” authorities.

anchor.surface_text: On 10 August 1997 she heard three gunshots outside her home. Subsequently, before she left for England, a real-estate agent came to meet her daughter and told her to sell their house and accept any offer he would make to buy it. The applicant believes that this real-estate agent was sent by the “TRNC” authorities to persuade her to leave the country.

facts.text: Following her application to the Court, the applicant's daughter was dismissed from a bank post and was not given a civil servant post despite ranking 15th among 68 candidates.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant further contends that following her application to the European Court of Human Rights, her daughter was dismissed from her post in a bank, and that although she was ranked 15th among 68 candidates in the examination to become a civil servant, she was not given a post.

facts.text: On 15 December 1999, the applicant met Professor Bakır Çağlar who allegedly told her she might be assassinated if she won her case and her daughter's scholarship would be discontinued.

anchor.surface_text: Moreover, the applicant's representatives informed the Court on 21 January 2000 that on 15 December 1999 the applicant had a meeting with Professor Bakır Çağlar about her application before the Court. Professor Çağlar, who is a former agent of the Turkish Government in the cases before the European Court of Human Rights, allegedly told the applicant that she might be assassinated if she won her case before the Court and that her daughter's scholarship would be discontinued.

facts.text: Kutlu Adalı was killed on 6 July 1996 at 11.40 p.m.; police received a tip-off and arrived promptly at the scene.

anchor.surface_text: 48.  The Government submit that on 6 July 1996 at 11.40 p.m. a tip-off was received at the communications section of the Lefkoşa Police Headquarters on telephone no. 155 from an unidentified caller, stating that there had been a murder at the point where Ardıç Street crosses Akasya Street.

facts.text: Police cordoned off the area and began investigation immediately; autopsy was carried out on 7 July 1996 by Dr İsmail Bundak.

anchor.surface_text: 50.  The investigation began immediately after the death of Kutlu Adalı. Early in the morning of 7 July 1996, at 3 a.m., police officers brought a doctor from the Nicosia (Lefkoşa) State Hospital to the scene of the incident. The doctor examined the body and established that Mr Adalı had died at the scene of the incident as a result of two bullet wounds in the areas of his left temple and left shoulder.

facts.text: Between 7 and 31 July 1996, police took statements from 59 persons including family members and neighbours.

anchor.surface_text: 51.  On 7 July 1996 police officers drew up a list of residents, including the applicant's neighbours, in the Akasya and Ardıç streets. On the same day statements were taken from thirty-three persons as to their knowledge about the incident. 53.  Between 8 and 31 July 1996 twenty-six further statements were taken from potential witnesses, including members of the applicant's family.

facts.text: Ballistic examination showed 14 cartridges were 9-mm Parabellum fired from a single gun at close range; weapon not linked to any known weapons in “TRNC”.

anchor.surface_text: 59.  A ballistic examination was also carried out on the used cartridges. Following the examination of 14 used cartridges, the ballistics report of 6 August 1996 stated that they were 9-mm Parabellum-type cartridges that had been fired from one single gun at close range. It was further noted in the report that the cartridges and the bullet cores were not linked to any other cartridges or bullet cores that had hitherto been found within the territory of the “TRNC” or recorded in the files on murders by unknown assailants.

facts.text: The investigation concluded on 4 March 1998 that the murderer(s) could not be identified and the case was closed by the coroner on 11 December 1998.

anchor.surface_text: 62.  On 4 March 1998 the police assistant inspector in charge of the investigation, Ahmet Soyalan, concluded his report on the investigation. In his concluding remarks, the inspector stated that it had not been possible to identify the murderer(s) and that he could not therefore reach a positive result for the investigation. 66.  The hearing in Lefkoşa before the coroner commenced on 20 October 1998 and, following statements from witnesses, was concluded on 11 December 1998 with the delivery of the verdict. The coroner found that Kutlu Adalı had been shot dead on 6 July 1996 by unidentified person(s), and that his death had been caused by organ dismemberment, internal haemorrhage and subdural haemorrhage in the head. The coroner stated that the murderer(s) of the deceased could not be identified and declared the case closed.
